newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU defends Lyonnais decision, no word on sell off.
newsitem.headline: EU defends Lyonnais decision, no word on sell off.

text.p: The European Commission on Thursday defended before Euro MEPs its decision to clear urgent aid to embattled Credit Lyonnais and declined to comment on France's pledge to sell the bank earlier than expected.

The Commission on Wednesday cleared emergency French aid of 3.9 billion french francs ($758 million) for state-controlled Lyonnais, pending the assessment of a third rescue package for the bank in three years.

"Credit Lyonnais will go down in history as a case where the Commission has bent its knee in the face of pressure from the French government," British Socialist Alan Donnelly told a meeting of the European Parliament's economic and monetary affairs committee.
But European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert reacted angrily to the accusation that the EU executive was being soft.
"The facts are on our side: we have been tough...we did not bend the rules because of pressure."
Van Miert also warned against jumping to the conclusion that the Commission would simply clear the bank's new rescue package, saying that it would not go without "real and substantive" divestments.

"No one can prejudge the outcome of the investigation of the case," he said the committee. Donnelly's harsh remark was isolated with most other members of the powerful committee adopting a rather restrained tone.

But Van Miert also stressed on Wednesday and again at the parliament the specificity of the case -- a huge company in a sector where failure of one of the main players could have devastating effects for the whole industry.
Credit Lyonnais was the first case of state aid in the banking sector the Commission had to deal with.

Advised by a group of former European central bank governors, it concluded at the time that the sector was "sensitive" and "specific" although it also said this did not mean it was exempted from EU competition rules.

In 1995, Credit Lyonnais, which was once the largest bank outside Japan, was allowed to receive a maximum of 45 billion French francs in subsidies as part of a long-term restructuring plan designed to get it back to profitability.

In return, the Commission ordered that it sell 35 percent of its foreign assets by the end of 1998 and carry part of the costs involved in transferring some 135 billion francs in shaky assets to a state-backed vehicle.

Van Miert has clearly implied the conditions were too tough in the context of a persistently depressed French financial market. He also implied the Commission was misled in 1995 by French rival banks which had said the rescue money would turn the Lyonnais into a "super champion'.

He told the parliament that the competitors -- mainly Societe Generale, which has challenged the Commission in the European court -- would have to explain how they also failed to assess the Lyonnais' situation properly.
Under the Commission's new investigation into the third rescue plan, interested parties will be again asked to give their views.
Van Miert declined to comment on French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis' pledge on Wednesday to privatise Lyonnais earlier than expected.
But he sounded doubtful that this would happen. "Did he say so?" Van Miert said with an amused look when asked by Reuters to react as he was leaving the parliament's meeting.
"There is no comment for the moment," Van Miert added.

On Wednesday he stressed that it was not so much when but whether the bank could be sold off quickly given its dire financial situation. The French government had originally said it would privatise Lyonnais around the year 2000.
($1=5.145 French Franc)
